wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A2:
ALL AROUND THE GLOBE
Samuel Coleman, the English comedian, is dead.

Forty thousand francs has been subscribed in Paris for the late fire in Quebec.

The strike of journeymen brewers at Cincinnati continues.

Fifteen hundred pilgrims visited the church of Notre Dame, Montreal, Sunday.

Gen. Weaver, greenback candidate for president last year, is on the stump in Nebraska.

Col, R. L. Mott, of Columbus Ga., was killed by the cars yesterday in the Union depot at Atlanta, Ga.

Dr. Emanuel Dreyfus, deputy coroner of New Orleans, has been indicted upon the charge of robbing a "stiff" of $150.

The proposed removal of the remains of Wm. Penn from England to Pennsylvania has been refused by the English trustees.

A fire in the lumber yards and mills at East Saginaw, Mich., destroyed property to the value of $150,000. Insurance $75,000.

Wash. Allen, a negro, in jail at Shreveport, La., charged with killing M. J. Scott, Saturday last, was taken out and hung by a mob last night.

Henry S. Smith who killed James Burton near Burnsville, Miss., in April, 1880, was hanged at Cornish yesterday in the presence of 5,000 people.

A tornado at New Jefferson, Harrison county, O., Saturday night, destroyed the Lutheran church and school house, unroofed many buildings, and killed a number of head of stock.

Billy, the Kid, a notorious murderer and outlaw, was shot and killed by Pat. Garrett, sheriff of Lincoln county, N. M., on the 14th. Garrett had been on the track of his game for several days.

The Lincoln national bank was organized in New York city yesterday with a capital of $300,000. With it is also incorporated the Grand Central deposit company. Mayor Grace is head of the enterprise.

During a drunken quarrel on Saturday between a number of Creek and Cherokee Indians, while holding an election barbecue, seven men were killed and wounded, two having their heads completely severed from their bodies.

The National Educational association met in session at Atlanta, Ga., yesterday. Two hundred delegates were in attendance, representing thirty States. In the evening the delegates were given a grand banquet by the citizens.

Miscellaneous.
CINCINNATI, July 20.—The Cincinnati Coffin Company's six story manufactory'and a large quantity of lumber was burned last night. Loss, $225,000; insured for $200,000.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., July 20.—Several mills and a large quantity of lumber was burned here yesterday. Loss about $160,000; insured for $75,000.

MILWAUKEE, July 12.—Over 1000 lumber mill laborers at Erie Clare and vicinity have struck for a reduction in hours from twelve to ten daily.

CINCINNATI, July 20.—The brewers' strike continues, but work progresses in all branches. The proprietors claim that they can fill the places of the strikers and suffer no inconvenience.

ST. LOUIS, July 20.—A Republican special from Shreveport, Louisiana, says: Wash Allen, a negro murderer, was taken from jail last evening by forty armed maskers and hanged.
wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A9:
A most atrocious crime was committed Saturday night at Kingston, a small hamlet in DeSoto parish, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield. Mr. Judd Scott, a young merchant doing business in Kingston left his boarding house about 9 o'clock p. m., going to his store where it was his custom to sleep. On Sunday morning his body was discovered lying about half way between Mrs. Beard's, where he boarded, and his store. The top of his head had been almost entirely blown off by a gun shot. The brains were scattered around, and hogs had partly devoured his body. His store and safe keys had been taken, and it was subsequently ascertained that the store and safe had been opened. No goods have been missed, and it is not known how much has been taken.

Mr Scott was one of the police jury-men in DeSoto parish, a man utterly without reproach and not known to have an enemy. the murder was evidently for the purpose of robbery.

Capt. Sample, sheriff of DeSoto parish, is on the ground and has arrested two negroes on strong circumstantial evidence. It is rumored this morning that an attempt was made last night to take the the prisoners from the sheriff for the purpose of lynching, but without success. Capt. Sample will protect the majesty of the law if posible, but it will be difficulty to restrain the people if the assassins are found. The citizens of DeSoto parish are determined to put down lawlessness.—Shreveport Standard.
wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A12:
The following letter received yesterday, gives some additional information concerning the murder, which has not been published until now:

MANSFIELD, July 19, 1881.

EDITOR TIMES.—Mr. M. J. Scott, a merchant and citizen of this parish, doing business at Kingston, was foully murdered on Saturday night, about 9 o'clock. He was at the time returning to the store from his boarding house, some two or three hundred yards distant with a lantern in his hand; was waylaid and shot in the back of the head, the shot entirely tearing away the back portion of the head, just as he was passing from the enclosure of his boarding-house. The news of this tragic event which reached us Sunday morning, was a great shock to the community. Mr. Scott was one of our best citizens and was not known to have an enemy in the world.

Sheriff Sample, with his usual energy and promptness, upon receipt of the first tidings, repaired to the scene of the tragedy and will probe the matter to the bottom, if it can be done. He sent to jail on Monday two negroes suspicioned of the crime. Last night the keys of the jail were forced from the jailor by some thirty or forty men presumed to reside in the vicinity of Kingston, and one of the prisoners, suspected, Wash Allen by name, was taken out, carried back to Kingston and hung there about daylight this morning. These men are generally known to be men of coolness and deliberation, and men who would not act hastily and without sufficient evidence. Allen is said to have confessed the crime before the hanging. The action of these gentlemen, so far as we have been able to learn, is approved in toto by the citizens of mansfield. It is idle to talk or think of the slow process of the law when so great a crime has been committed. Robbery was the incentive to the murder. All facts point to this conclusion. In this the murderer failed entirely. Very truly, JOSEPH JONES.
wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A13:
THE SCOTT MURDER.
A Full Confession Made by Wash Allen, Whose Case, Was Dispos ed of by Judge Lynch
Shreveport Times.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. McDeavreaux, driver of the Mansfield stage, brought information to the effect that the negro, Wash Allen, who was taken from the Mansfield jail Monday night by 30 or 40 masked men and hung at Kingston, the particulars of which were given yesterday by the Times, made a clean breast of the whole affair, implicating four or five others, and informed the crowd where the gun with which he committed the terrible deed could be found and detailed the manner in which the whole affair was conducted.

The parties—all negroes—implicated by Allen were arrested Tuesday and taken to Manfield and confined in the parish jail.

The gun was found at the very spot where Allen said he had secreted it, and on the locks were found blood and hair of the murdered man. He stated that the killing of Mr. Scott was a prearranged affair and the four or five others, whom he implicated, stood guard while he did the shooting, and after he had fired the fatal shot, to make death doubly sure, he approached the prostrate form of Mr. Scott and dealt him several heavy blows with the gun, crushing in the forehead.

The excitement at Mansfield was at fever heat and lynching of all the parties connected with the murder was freely talked of. Sheriff Sample and his deputies were taking every precaution to protect the prisoners, but we doubt if they have or will be able to save them from the swift and just punishment meted out to Wash Allen. SUMMARY OF STATE NEWS.
Gleanings from the Louisiana Press
Gleanings from the Louisiana Press
Minden Democrat: Saturday night as Mr. M. Judd Scott, of Kingston, a little place a few miles north of Mansfield, was going from the house where he boarded, to his store, a distance of about 250 yards, he was shot and instantly killed. The murder was not found out until next morning when his body was found riddled with buckshot. The murderers rifled his pockets, went to his store and took fifty or sixty dollars that was in the drawer, but were unable to get the safe open. A Negro named Wash Allen was suspicioned as being one of the parties. His house was searched, resulting in the finding of a watch and several articles of clothing belonging to Mr. Scott; also a pair of pants that the murderer wore the previous day which were stained with blood. He was taken to Mansfield and incarcerated. At night an armed body of men rode into town and aroused the deputy Sheriff, informing him that they had a prisoner they wished to lock up. The Sheriff went to the jail, when they immediately overpowered and took the key from him. They then unlocked the cell, took out the Negro and went off with him. The next morning he was found hanging to a limb a few yards from where the crime was committed. Other parties are implicated. Investigation in progress.

Shreveport Standard: Sunday week during church service at Grand Cane City, on the line of the New Orleans Pacific, in DeSoto parish, the store of Messrs. Peyton & Burrow was broken open by one Donglass, a railroad hand, and about $400 in money stolen. Donglass was arrested and the
one Douglass, a railroad hand, and about $400 in money stolen. Douglass was arrested and the money subsequently recovered at the spot where he had hidden it away. A colored man named Philip Jackson was shot and mortally wounded while sitting in front of the house of Dave Barnhill, in the Lake country. Jackson was in company with some five or six men and women talking, when suddenly a gun went off at the fence, some twenty feet from the house, and Jackson fell pierced with several buckshot, slugs and pieces of lead. Suspicion rests on two colored men, one of whom is the paramour of Jackson's wife, and had induced her to leave him. The authorities are after the suspected parties.

Claiborne Guardian: The cotton worm appeared on Red river much earlier than usual this year, but the chrysalis was destroyed by the heat or by some insect or bird. A large planter near Shreveport told the writer that he found numbers so destroyed. His conclusion was that no serious damage would be done the crop. Deputy Sheriff, I. N. Glover, captured Sunday morning, two miles below Vienna, Charlie Johnson and Sarah Coleman, who had murdered Squire Coleman near Shreveport, a short time since. Mr. Glover left with the prisoners for Shreveport. John Cupp of this parish was robbed last Thursday Thursday night of $1300. Mr. Cupp was away from home at the time. The house was entered and the money taken out, showing that the robbery must have been committed by some person familiar with the house.
wash-allen-shreveport-1881-07-19.A24: THE HORRORS OF. LYNCH LAW.—The negro Wash Allen, who was lynched for the murder of Mr. M. J. Scott at Kingston, was swung up sixteen or eighteen times to extort a confession from him. When taken down he told a disconnected story and implicated other negroes, who clearly proved an alibi. Several times the hardened wretch laughed in the face of the party after he was let down, and never begged for mercy, though he asked to be shot. Sheriff Sample says he was one of the most intractable prisoners he ever had in charge.—Shreveport (La.) Times.
